summary: The q²+1 count is folklore and was already re-derived in reviews/triage-brainstorm-B.md, which also corrects it in characteristic 2. I did the cheap version of the first step: regressing log M_BM(p) (the BM-corrected main term, BM_CORRECTED_COUNT §2) and log(U+1) on (q/p), q < 80, over 1600 primes p ≡ 1 (4) in (100, 30000). M_BM gets the sign right only at q ≤ 7 (q·β = −0.18, −0.10, −0.08, −0.04 against U's −0.37, −0.35, −0.49, −0.09) and misses the q ≡ 2 (3) pattern entirely (q = 11, 17, 23: M_BM +0.03, +0.04, +0.13 against U −0.34, −0.33, −0.18), so the BM main term does not explain the fitted per-prime weights (EVIDENCE).

Bradford–Ionascu Conj. 1.1 (arXiv:1405.4025, read) allows denominators in Q1 ∪ Q3, a cone that contains −ℕ. On the real axis it is therefore trivial (4/(4k+1) = 1/k − 1/(k(4k+1))), contrary to BRAINSTORM/other_rings.md §4, which calls it a 'lottery again'. An exhaustive search (CERTIFIED by the search) found a solution for all 1614 first-quadrant n with N(n) ≤ 2000. The sharper closed-Q1-only cone contains ES exactly as its real slice (PROVED: Im(1/a) ≤ 0 forces real denominators); exhaustive search to N(n) ≤ 4000 finds exactly 12 exceptions, 6 up to n ↦ i·n̄: 2+5i, 3+4i = (2+i)², 4+5i, 5+6i, 10+13i, 2+17i, all of norm ≤ 293 (EVIDENCE of a finite exceptional set). This is a strict strengthening of ES with no new mechanism, so it gives no lever on ES.

Matrix ES for k = 2 is trivially solvable for every n by one identity (PROVED). A = [[2,1],[1,1]] and B = [[1,−1],[−1,2]] are unimodular and positive definite with A + B + I = 4I, so X = nA⁻¹, Y = nB⁻¹, Z = nI are integral positive-definite matrices with X⁻¹ + Y⁻¹ + Z⁻¹ = (4/n)I. Projecting gives numerators ≠ 1 (e.g. 2/n), so nothing transfers to ES.

At every (★) hit p = 4uBC − u − B we have (−uB/p) = −1, so (−uB)^{(p−1)/4} = ±i₀, with i₀ = a/b mod p for p = a² + b² (a odd, b even, both positive). Over 8964 primes p ≡ 1 (4) ≤ 2·10⁵ the split is 48206 / 48199 (+i₀ / −i₀). Every subgroup (p mod 8, p mod 16, (2/p)₄) is within 1.3σ of 1/2, as is a random-A control (13367 / 13492), and the per-prime fraction has mean 0.5003 (EVIDENCE: no quartic bias, consistent with BRAINSTORM/apollonian_reciprocity.md).

Pomerance–Weingartner (arXiv:2511.16817 v2, Table 1, read) sieved 8/n up to 10¹³ (ET's seven congruences, with 4 replaced by m). The only exceptions are n = 1, 2, 3, 11, 17, 131, 241, so the 'extend to 10⁶' step is done in the literature (17 and 241 are the only ones ≡ 1 mod 4). The repo's 8/p data agree (BRAINSTORM/s8_numerator_size_screen.md; data/z52b/raw/m8_pr1e5.txt; BRAINSTORM/y7_mordell_levels.md, whose 8/n covering at level 840 leaves all 6 squares plus 17 other classes uncovered). A covering-family proof of all-even ES is blocked by the square classes, which the M = 8 covering leaves uncovered (y7_mordell_levels: the M = 8 core contains all 6 unit squares), as for m = 4.

The coincidence is explained by a trivial lemma, not a deeper equivalence. An all-even solution forces some denominator ≡ 0 (mod 4) (PROVED: if all v₂ = 1, halving gives 8/p = Σ1/a_i with the a_i odd, and the parity of p(ab+bc+ca) = 8abc is contradictory). So failures of the '4 | some denominator' condition lie inside the 8/p failures, which up to 10¹³ are {17, 241} among p ≡ 1 (4) (Pomerance–Weingartner Table 1); by direct enumeration 17 and 241 have no solution with 4 | a denominator. The two failure sets therefore coincide up to 10¹³, but there is no per-solution bijection: 233 has 15 solutions with 4 | some denominator but only 9 all-even.

The first step (the mod-840 uncovered classes for m = 5 after the small Type I/II identities) is already in BRAINSTORM/y7_mordell_levels.md. That table, PROVED by exhaustive enumeration, leaves 2 unit classes for M = 5 at L = 840, namely n ≡ 1 (mod 420), against Mordell's 6 squares for M = 4. The alternative step (Type I/II at odd squares for m = 5) is in BRAINSTORM/ident_numerators.md §4: odd squares carry Type I/II solutions for m = 5. Pomerance–Weingartner verify m = 5 to 10¹⁸.

I tabulated the largest prime exception P(m) ≤ 10⁵ and the exception counts for m = 5..48 from the existing raw counts (main checkout data/z52b/raw/m*_pr1e5.txt). The table matches PW Table 1 for m ≤ 15 (e.g. 241, 12241, 281, 353, 20521). For m ≥ 24 exceptions reach the top of the range (saturated). On the unsaturated m, log P(m) ≈ m^0.74 and the mean count at p ≈ 7.5·10⁴ scales as m^−1.19 (EVIDENCE, small-m noisy). The literature (PW, m ≤ 30000) already supersedes this, and the table gives no ES-specific lever.

Rav's criterion, applied to the remainder (4x − p)/(px), is the window/cap-0 divisor condition. The proposed Cauchy–Davenport/Kneser certifier on D = {d mod m : d | K} is exactly BRAINSTORM/s6_divisor_pigeonhole.md. That memo proves a pigeonhole criterion and a Cauchy–Davenport sharpness result and tests them numerically to 2·10⁵: the criterion fires for 4870 of 8977 primes at the least forced window, and it needs Ω(K) ≳ q/4, i.e. it is linear in q (B3). See also B2_ACROSS_FIELDS row 9. The smallest-x alternative is greedy_algorithm_dynamics.md Prop B.2 (see Z0148).

1/x + 1/y + 1/z = 4/w is NOT partition regular (PROVED by the Rado necessity argument transposed to reciprocals). Colour n by the residue mod a large prime ℓ of its ℓ-free part; a monochromatic solution then forces a zero-sum subset of the coefficients (1, 1, 1, −4), and there is none. This matches Lefmann's reciprocal Rado theory (JCTA 1991, Thm 2.1, as quoted by Chapman arXiv:2210.04347). The result does not bear on ES, which concerns every fixed n rather than colourings.

For S = {2,3,5,7} I classified exactly which primes p admit 4/p = Σ1/x_i with every x_i ∈ U ∪ pU (PROVED reduction: either p = numerator of 4 − 1/s₁ − 1/s₂, or p = (4u − 1)/v with u/v = s₂s₃/(s₂ + s₃)). The search covers 17101 of the 78494 primes ≤ 10⁶, including 7818 of the p ≡ 1 (4). The covered fraction decays steadily: 0.92 on (10³, 2·10³], 0.54 on (1.6·10⁴, 3.2·10⁴], 0.14 on (5·10⁵, 10⁶]. This fits the polylog count ≪ (log X)^{2|S|} of S-unit expressions, so it is a density-zero lottery for each fixed S.

4/n = 1/a² + 1/b² + 1/c² forces 4 | n (PROVED, 2-adic). If W = max v₂ of the denominators is attained once or three times, v₂(n) = 2W + 2; if twice, v₂(n) = 2W + 1 with W ≥ 1. So no odd n, in particular no prime, is representable. The problem is really 1/m = Σ1/a_i² with n = 4m and has no ES content. An exhaustive search for n ≤ 3000 finds 80 representable n, all multiples of 4 (12, 16, 24, 32, 48, …).

The first step is settled by parity: all-odd denominators are impossible at odd n (PROVED). The 2-adic pattern question is answered in BRAINSTORM/y4_oneodd_slices.md via (J)32 Lemma 2.1: every ES solution at odd n is either all-even (the 8/n slice) or has exactly one odd denominator. Lemma 1 there gives the slot-level v₂ criterion (v₂(X) = 2 ⇔ one-odd, ≥ 3 ⇔ all-even) and cell tables mod 8. The Breusch/Stewart length question for odd denominators is unrelated to the 3-term problem.

Bounded look-ahead greedy is BRAINSTORM/greedy_algorithm_dynamics.md Prop B.2 (PROVED dictionary): with x = ⌈p/4⌉ + j, J(p) = (a_min(p) − 3)/4, the window statistic of POINTWISE_SIZE §8. J/log p < 2.5 is verified to 10⁸ (EVIDENCE), the distribution to 3·10⁵ is there (max J(118801) = 14), and no fixed J suffices (CONDITIONAL on Dickson). The records of 4x(p) − p are OEIS A400619 (cf. Z0932).

The equivalence ES(n) ⇔ a hyperbolic triangle orbifold with χ = −1 + 4/n is a known restatement: it is spelled out on MathOverflow 267209 ('one can realize −1 + 4/n iff the Erdős–Straus conjecture'). A web search found no theorem on which rationals are triangle-orbifold Euler characteristics. Riemann–Hurwitz for covers of S²(x, y, z) only rescales χ, so no new constraint appears. The arithmetic (Takeuchi) subcase is Z0168.

I checked the dictionary: for M(0; (x,1), (y,1), (z,1)), e = −(1/x + 1/y + 1/z) and |H₁| = |xyz·e| = xy + yz + zx = det P(x, y, z), so ES(n) ⇔ some positive pretzel P(x, y, z) has det = 4xyz/n. This is a restatement. The suggested T1/sliceness link is void: P(x, y, z) with x, y, z > 0 is alternating with nonzero signature, so it is never slice, and Greene–Jabuka's classification has no positive cases to offer. Linking forms and Alexander polynomials depend on (x, y, z) alone, not on any arithmetic of n beyond the equation itself.

Kawamura (arXiv:2606.27104, verified title: 'Proof of the Density Threshold Conjecture for Pinwheel Scheduling') proves that every pinwheel instance of density ≤ 5/6 is schedulable. ES triples have density 4/n ≤ 4/5 < 5/6 (n ≥ 5), so they are always schedulable and the theorem carries no information about which densities are realised by three unit fractions. This is a restatement only.

I reconstructed Takeuchi's list computationally from his trace criterion, recovering exactly 85 groups (76 cocompact). Intersecting with 1/a + 1/b + 1/c = 4/n gives only the finite set n ∈ {5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 16, 18, 20}, plus n ∈ {6, 8, 12} from noncocompact triples with ∞ entries. The only prime is n = 5, via (2, 5, 10). So arithmetic triangle groups contribute nothing beyond tiny n.
